title: The imperative and prohibitions

objectives.can: Recognise second- and third-person imperatives, present and aorist, and parse them.
Read the two forms of prohibition: μή with the present imperative and μή with the aorist subjunctive.

explanation.summary: The imperative is the mood of commands, requests and permissions. It has second and third persons, and a present and an aorist tense-form that differ in aspect. A prohibition, a negative command, is made in two ways: μή with a present imperative, or μή with an aorist subjunctive.

sections.heading: What the imperative does
body: The imperative addresses the will. It can order, forbid, request, invite or permit, and the tone comes from the situation, not from the form. In Matthew 5:16 οὕτως λαμψάτω τὸ φῶς ὑμῶν says that the light is to shine: the speaker is giving a direction. The same mood is used in prayer and in the language of the household; it is neither rude nor harsh in itself.

The imperative exists in the second person, to those addressed, and in the third person. The third person gives what English tries to say with 'let': λαμψάτω is 'let it shine', and in John 14:27 μὴ ταρασσέσθω … ἡ καρδία is 'let the heart not be troubled'. There is no first person imperative; for 'let us', Greek uses the hortatory subjunctive of the last lessons.

sections.heading: Recognising the forms
body: The present imperative is built on the present stem, and the aorist on the aorist stem, with no augment. Learn the second person singular first. In the active, the present has the bare stem with -ε (πίστευε, λέγε) and the aorist adds -σον (πίστευσον). Contract verbs contract the vowel in the usual way (ποίει). The second aorist uses the aorist stem with the ending -ε, and a few common verbs, among them λέγω and ἔρχομαι, put the accent on the ending in the grammars' paradigm: εἰπέ, ἐλθέ. Editions do not always accent the others of this group in the same way.

In the middle and passive the second person singular of the present ends in -ου (ἅπτου, φοβοῦ, πορεύου); the first aorist middle has -σαι; and the aorist passive has -θητι. The third person has -τω in the singular and -τωσαν in the plural: -έτω in the present, -σάτω in the first aorist, -θήτω in the aorist passive; middle and passive have -έσθω and -σάσθω. The second person plural has the ending -τε and is the same as the indicative in the present: πιστεύετε can be 'you believe' or 'believe!', and in a mood that has the same form only the context decides. The aorist imperative has no augment, which separates it from the indicative: -σατε against ἠκούσατε-type forms with an augment.

sections.heading: Present and aorist: aspect, not time
body: As in the subjunctive, the tense-form of the imperative shows aspect and not time. A command is always aimed at the time after it is given. The present imperative sees the action as going on, repeated or habitual; the aorist sees it as a whole, often a single act to be carried out. In Luke 8:50 μὴ φοβοῦ is a present imperative and μόνον πίστευσον an aorist; in Mark 5:36 the same words have the present πίστευε. Both are natural, and the difference is slight. In John 2:16 Jesus uses an aorist for the single act of taking the doves away (Ἄρατε) and a present in the prohibition that follows (μὴ ποιεῖτε).

Do not translate the aspect as if it were a rule. 'Keep doing' is a possible sense of the present imperative but not its definition: very many present imperatives are simply general commands, and very many aorists are not about a single moment.

sections.heading: Two ways to forbid
body: Greek forbids in the second person in two ways, both with the negative μή. The first is μή with the present imperative: μὴ φοβεῖσθε in Matthew 10:31, μὴ κωλύετε in Mark 9:39, 1 Thessalonians 5:19 τὸ πνεῦμα μὴ σβέννυτε. The second is μή with the aorist subjunctive: μὴ φοβηθῆτε in Matthew 10:26, μὴ νομίσητε in Matthew 5:17, μὴ μεριμνήσητε in Matthew 6:34. A prohibition in the second person is not normally made with μή and the aorist imperative.
A prohibition in the third person uses μή with an imperative, present or aorist: μὴ ταρασσέσθω in John 14:27, μὴ καταβάτω in Mark 13:15. The subjunctive is not used for it.

Why two forms? The aspect of the verb shows through. The present imperative tends to be used for a general instruction, for a habit, or for something that has begun; the aorist subjunctive tends to be used for a particular act or occasion, or when the whole action is in view. Grammars of the older kind taught that μή with the present imperative means 'stop doing' and μή with the aorist subjunctive means 'do not start'. That is only a tendency, and the New Testament has many verses which it does not fit. In Matthew 6:25 Jesus says μὴ μεριμνᾶτε (present imperative) and in 6:31 μὴ μεριμνήσητε (aorist subjunctive) about the same worry, in the same speech. Nothing in the text says that the hearers had been worrying in one verse and not in the other. In Matthew 10 the same verb appears in both forms in a few verses: μὴ φοβηθῆτε in 10:26, μὴ φοβεῖσθε in 10:28 and 10:31. Read each prohibition in its own context before deciding what the form adds.

misunderstandings: Taking every second person plural -ετε as a statement. Without context, πιστεύετε, κωλύετε and ποιεῖτε are indicative or imperative. The negative μή (in place of οὐ), and the setting of a command, show the imperative.

Treating μή with the present imperative as always meaning 'stop doing it'. Many such prohibitions are general rules (Matthew 7:1, 1 Thessalonians 5:19) and say nothing about what the hearers have been doing.
Treating μή with the aorist subjunctive as a different mood of command. It is a prohibition like the other, in the subjunctive form, and it does not state a wish or a doubt.
Reading the aorist imperative as a command about the past. It has no augment and no past time; like the present, it looks forward to the action commanded.

deeper.heading: Why the aorist imperative is not used after μή
body: In the second person, Greek keeps the aorist imperative for positive commands and uses the aorist subjunctive for the negative. Grammarians describe this as a habit of the language, and explain it in different ways; the pattern μή + aorist subjunctive became the usual way of forbidding with the aorist. The third person with the aorist imperative remained possible, as Mark 13:15 shows.

deeper.heading: Debated cases
body: Some verses are disputed. In John 20:17 Μή μου ἅπτου is a present imperative after μή, and interpreters have taken it as 'stop clinging to me' and as 'do not touch me'. The Greek form allows both, because the present imperative with μή does not by itself say whether the action had begun. The reading depends on the scene, not on a rule of grammar.

paradigms.title: Imperative endings
paradigms.caption: Add them to the present or the aorist stem. The aorist has no augment.

paradigms.note: The second aorist active takes the present endings on the aorist stem: -ε, -έτω, -ετε, -έτωσαν. A few common second aorists carry the accent on the ending in the second person singular: εἰπέ, ἐλθέ.
